title: Initial Value Problems, Existence and Uniqueness
short: Know when exactly one solution passes through a point.
trouble: Students assume every initial value problem has exactly one solution, missing cases like y′ = √y with y(0) = 0.

blocks.html: An initial value problem (IVP) pairs an equation $y' = f(t, y)$ with a starting value $y(t_0) = y_0$. In Direction Fields and Euler's Method you traced a curve from a point by following the slopes. It is natural to assume exactly one curve leaves each point. Usually that is true, but not always, and the exceptions are worth knowing.

Theorem. If $f$ and $\partial f/\partial y$ are continuous on a rectangle containing $(t_0, y_0)$, then the IVP has exactly one solution on some interval around $t_0$.
Linear case. For $y' + p(t)y = g(t)$, if $p$ and $g$ are continuous on an open interval $I$ containing $t_0$, the unique solution exists on all of $I$.

Suppose $y_1$ and $y_2$ both solve the IVP and let $w = y_1 - y_2$, so $w(t_0) = 0$. By the mean value theorem, $$w' = f(t, y_1) - f(t, y_2) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(t, \xi)\,w$$ for some $\xi$ between $y_1$ and $y_2$. If $|\partial f/\partial y| \le K$, then $|w|$ can grow at most like $|w(t_0)|e^{K|t - t_0|} = 0$. A bounded $\partial f/\partial y$ keeps two solutions from peeling apart. When $\partial f/\partial y$ blows up, that protection is gone.

blocks.title: Two solutions from one point
steps: In fact $y = 0$ until any time $c \ge 0$, followed by $y = (t - c)^{3}$, is also a solution: infinitely many.
Here $\partial f/\partial y = 2y^{-1/3}$, which is undefined at $y = 0$, so the theorem never promised uniqueness.
blocks.a: The IVP has more than one solution.

blocks.html: Assuming every initial value problem has exactly one solution. For $y' = \sqrt{y}$ with $y(0) = 0$, both $y = 0$ and $y = \frac{t^{2}}{4}$ (for $t \ge 0$) work. Before trusting a single answer, check the hypotheses: are $f$ and $\partial f/\partial y$ continuous at the starting point? Here $\partial f/\partial y = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}$ is not.

For a linear equation the answer comes from the coefficients alone: divide by the leading coefficient to reach standard form, list every $t$ where $p$ or $g$ is undefined or discontinuous, and take the gap that contains $t_0$.

blocks.title: The interval for a linear IVP
blocks.q: On what interval is the solution of $(t - 3)y' + (\ln t)y = 2t$, $y(1) = 2$, guaranteed to exist and be unique?
steps: The trouble points split the line into $(0, 3)$ and $(3, \infty)$; $t_0 = 1$ lies in $(0, 3)$.

blocks.title: A short life without any trouble point
blocks.q: Does $y' = y^{2}$, $y(0) = 1$ have a unique solution, and for how long?
steps: $f = y^{2}$ and $\partial f/\partial y = 2y$ are continuous everywhere, so there is exactly one solution near $t = 0$.
It blows up as $t \to 1^{-}$, even though the equation looks perfectly smooth.
blocks.a: Unique, but it exists only for $t < 1$. For nonlinear equations the theorem promises just some interval.

blocks.name: slopefield
blocks.cap: Slopes of $y' = 3y^{2/3}$. The blue curve from $(0, 0)$ stays on the equilibrium $y = 0$, while the teal curves, shifted copies of $y = (t - c)^{3}$, leave the same line with slope 0. Several solutions touch at each point of $y = 0$.
